extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of aesthetics, artists, writers, and poets interested in the sublime and beautiful
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts principles for producing and evaluating the sublime and the beautiful in art, literature, architecture, and sensory experience, as argued in an 18th-century philosophical treatise. Focuses on sensory causes (light, colour, texture, motion, size, taste, words) and their emotional effects (terror/astonishment for the sublime; relaxation/love for the beautiful).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects of Blackness
rubrics_metrics.description: BLACKNESS is but a partial darkness; black bodies, reflecting none or but a few rays, are like vacant spaces dispersed among objects. When the eye lights on one of these vacuities after being kept in tension by adjacent colours, it suddenly relaxes and then recovers by a convulsive spring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blackness produces a sudden relaxation followed by a convulsive motion because of an unexpected change of sensory stimulation. Examples given: misjudging a chair's height, taking an extra stair step, sudden darkness waking a person inclined to sleep, sudden cessation of murmuring sounds. Effect on mind/body: startle, melancholy, terror. Use black (or sudden darkness) to create shock, melancholy, or to interrupt relaxation; anticipate moderation by context and custom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects of Blackness Moderated
rubrics_metrics.description: Though the effects of black may be painful originally, custom reconciles us; after being used to black objects, terror abates and smoothness or glossiness can soften the horror, yet black will always retain something melancholy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Black combined with agreeable accidents (gloss, smoothness) can moderate its sternness. If black occupies the whole field of sight it becomes darkness and follows the rules previously given for darkness. Do not assume black's effect is uniform; habituation and combinations with other colours alter impact. The author stops short of exhaustive classification—use these leading principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical Cause of Love
rubrics_metrics.description: When presented with objects that excite love and complacency, the body relaxes: head reclines, eyelids partly closed, eyes roll gently towards the object, mouth slightly open, slow breath with low sighs, hands fall idly, accompanied by a sense of melting and languor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This bodily relaxation, proportioned to degree of beauty and sensibility, is the physical basis of the passion called love. The author argues beauty acts by relaxing the fibres; conversely, passion originating in the mind will produce corresponding outward relaxation. Use descriptions of bodily relaxation to evoke or signal love/positive pleasure in writing or art; consider gradation and exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Why Smoothness is Beautiful
rubrics_metrics.description: Smoothness causes positive pleasure by relaxing the organs of touch, taste, smell, and hearing; therefore it is a principal constituent of visual beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rough and angular bodies rouse and vellicate the organs, causing pain via violent tension; smooth application (gentle stroking, smooth bed) relaxes and induces sleep or pleasure. Apply smoothness across senses to increase perceived beauty; roughness/pungency are associated with strengthening/tension rather than beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sweetness (its nature)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sweetness in taste arises from smooth liquid vehicles (water, oil) combined with a specific salt (sugar) which puts the nervous papillae into a gentle vibratory motion; sugar's particles are spherical and thus produce a smooth, agreeable sensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: round/smooth particles (like marbles) produce pleasurable tactile motion when they slide over each other. Water and oil are insipid but slightly sweet due to smoothness; sugar's larger spherical particles intensify this. Use the analogy of microscopic smoothness and motion to justify why certain tastes feel 'beautiful' and relaxing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sweetness is Relaxing
rubrics_metrics.description: Sweet things (and sweet smells) are generally relaxing; frequent or large intake of sweet/oily substances weakens stomach tone, sweet smells (flowers) dispose to drowsiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Languages often conflate 'soft' and 'sweet' (e.g., French doux). Early natural provisions (milk, fruit) are sweet and relaxing, suggesting sweetness may be the originally pleasant taste. In contrast, strengthening substances tend to be rough or pungent. Use sweet textures/smells/tastes in description to suggest relaxation, softness, and early/innate pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variation: why beautiful
rubrics_metrics.description: A principal property of beautiful objects is that the line of their parts is continually varying in direction by very insensible deviations; it never varies so quickly as to surprise or cause twitching of the optic nerve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neither long monotony nor sharp sudden variation is beautiful because both oppose agreeable relaxation. Gentle oscillatory motion (rising and falling), gradual waves, and continually varied variation relax attention and are pleasurable (examples: rocking a child, a smooth coach ride). Avoid sharp angles, sudden inequalities, and long unvarying repetition. The variation itself must be continually varied—use subtle, non-jarring changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concerning Smallness (size and beauty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas of great and small are relative to species; smallness per se has nothing contrary to beauty and may enhance it if proportions and delicacy fit the size; great magnitude typically aligns with the sublime, not the beautiful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive greatness often produces terror/awesomeness (sublime) and overrules qualities of beauty. Extremely small things can be beautiful (hummingbird), but dwarfish proportions in humans may be disagreeable. In narrative/art, use scale deliberately: large scale tends to inspire awe/terror (sublime), smallness can amplify delicacy and love, but beware of unusualness being read as monstrous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Of Colour (transparency, even reflection, and pleasure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Transparent bodies that transmit light softly and reflect their proper colour evenly produce a smooth visual pleasure; opaque particulates interrupt rays and produce disagreeable effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pleasure from colour compounds the softness of transmitted light and the evenness of reflected light. The shape of a vessel presenting a transparent colour can heighten pleasure by gradual interchange of strength and weakness of the colour. Use transparency, even reflection, and gradual variation to create visual beauty; particulate interruption causes displeasure (analogy with muddy liquor versus clear transparent liquor).

rubrics_metrics.name: Painting, Architecture, and Proportion
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural objects affect by laws of nature; painting affects similarly with the added pleasure of imitation; architecture affects by laws of nature and reason, from which rules of proportion derive that determine praise or censure relative to a work's intended end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or producing architecture or painting, consider both natural/sensory causes and rational rules (proportion, purpose). Proportion should serve the intended function; failures in proportion are grounds for censure. Use imitation in painting and reasoned proportion in architecture to achieve desired emotional effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Words affect by sound and association (poetry and eloquence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Words do not always affect the mind by raising clear ideas of the things they stand for; especially compound abstract words (virtue, honour) function largely as sounds imbued by habit with the effects of their past occasions rather than by producing precise representative ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Words are classed into aggregate (man, tree), simple abstract (red, round), and compound abstract (virtue, honour). Compound abstracts rarely produce distinct ideas on hearing; their power comes from habitual association with occasions that produced pleasure or pain. In poetry and rhetoric, employ words (especially general/abstract ones) for their associative emotional force and habitual residues, not merely for descriptive precision. Be aware children learn general words (virtue/vice) before particulars—so tone and apparent approval/disapproval can shape affective response.
